segs.text: Module three, objective three. Determining optimum dosing for an infused drug by calculating its parameters. Dosing an infusion means choosing the infusion rate, R, and when needed a loading dose, so that C p, the plasma concentration, sits at a target. A loading dose is an I V bolus given as the infusion starts, sized to reach the target at once. Before either can be chosen, the stem's data have to be turned into three parameters: k, the fraction of drug removed per hour; V D, the apparent volume of distribution, which relates the amount in the body to C p; and the clearance, the volume of plasma emptied of drug per hour.

card.m: choices: R and a loading dose, for a target C<sub>p</sub>
loading dose: I V bolus at the start
k: hr<sup>−1</sup>; V<sub>D</sub>: L; Cl: L/hr

segs.text: Clearance and V D belong to the patient: the textbook treats them as the independent parameters, and k as depending on both. R and the loading dose are the clinician's choices. Each choice follows one patient parameter: the rate follows the clearance, because the plateau is R over clearance, and the loading dose follows V D, because it is the amount that brings that volume to the target level. The textbook describes the clinical routine: start a rate from published values, measure C p twice with the second sample near steady state, then recompute k and adjust the rate.

card.m: patient: Cl and V<sub>D</sub>; k depends on both
start R → two samples → recompute k → adjust R

segs.text: Clearance equals k times V D. k is the fraction of the volume emptied each hour, so multiplying it by the volume gives the liters emptied each hour. Read the other way, k is clearance over V D: a larger clearance removes a larger fraction each hour, and the same clearance acting on a larger volume removes a smaller fraction, so the half-life is longer. Any two of the three give the third, and this line is not on the equation sheet. When the stem gives the routes separately, total body clearance, Cl T, is renal plus metabolic clearance: in her Practice four, five plus six point five five is eleven point five five liters per hour.

card.m: k = {{frac:Cl|V<sub>D</sub>}}: Cl larger → k larger; V<sub>D</sub> larger → k smaller, t<sub>½</sub> longer
any two → the third; not on the sheet

segs.text: Her renal failure parts show what each parameter does. In Practice four the clearance falls from eleven point five five to eight point five five liters per hour while V D stays one hundred liters. So k falls from zero point one one five five to zero point zero eight five five per hour, and the half-life lengthens from six to about eight point one hours. To keep the same target of ten milligrams per liter, R falls in proportion to the clearance, from one hundred fifteen point five to eighty five point five milligrams per hour. The loading dose, ten milligrams per liter times one hundred liters, stays one thousand milligrams, because clearance is not in it.

card.m: D<sub>L</sub> = 10 mg/L × 100 L = 1000 mg, both times

segs.text: Her slide Example one asks the expected C s s, the steady state concentration, for theophylline infused at fifty milligrams per hour, with a half-life of six hours and a V D of thirty liters. C s s is R over clearance, because the plateau is where the rate in equals the clearance times the level. The stem gives no clearance, so the half-life becomes k, and k times the volume becomes the clearance. Dividing the rate by that clearance gives fourteen point four three milligrams per liter, which she works with as fourteen point four. While working this aloud she called the thirty liters the clearance; thirty liters is V D, and the clearance is k times thirty liters.

card.m: t<sub>½</sub> = 6 hr, V<sub>D</sub> = 30 L, R = 50 mg/hr; C<sub>ss</sub> = ?

segs.text: Her slide Examples three and four give clearance directly: Cl T is four point five liters per hour, k is zero point one five per hour, and the rate is fifty milligrams per hour. C s s is fifty over four point five, eleven point one one milligrams per liter. C p eight hours after the start is that plateau times the fraction reached, one minus e to the minus k t. The result, seven point seven six milligrams per liter, is about seventy percent of the plateau, which fits: the half-life is four point six two hours, so eight hours lies between one and two half-lives, between fifty and seventy five percent. She did not say this value aloud; it is computed from her R, Cl T and k.

card.m: Cl<sub>T</sub> = 4.5 L/hr, k = 0.15 hr<sup>−1</sup>, R = 50 mg/hr
t<sub>½</sub> = 4.62 hr; 8 hr = 1.73 half-lives: between 50% and 75% ✓

segs.text: How she tests it: one patient in the stem, then six to nine chained parts, and later parts say at the rate you determined above, so an error in k carries into every later answer. Her graded quiz gave only a V D of twenty two liters and a clearance of three point two liters per hour, so k had to be built as clearance over V D before the level five hours after stopping could be found. Weight may come in pounds and V D per kilogram: one hundred ten pounds is fifty kilograms, and three liters per kilogram then gives one hundred fifty liters.

card.m: quiz: k = {{frac:3.2 L/hr|22 L}} = 0.1455 hr−1; 14 mg/L → 6.8 mg/L 5 hr after stopping

segs.text: Some data are never used, such as the age and sex in her quiz and the sixty five kilogram weight in Practice four. Contrasting scenarios are set in capitals, with the loading dose against without the loading dose, so check which one each part means. She computes to more precision than she reports and rounds to a practical value, for example fourteen point eight six milligrams per hour to fifteen. Micrograms per milliliter equal milligrams per liter, so a target in either unit goes straight into these lines. With k, V D and the clearance set, objective six chooses the rate, objective four the loading dose, and objective seven the level at any time.
